hero.subtitle: The foundational design philosophy behind the Internet's architecture

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes the fundamental architectural principles that guided the design of the Internet. These principles explain why the Internet works the way it does and provide guidance for future protocol design.

Understanding these principles is essential for anyone designing Internet protocols or distributed systems. They represent decades of collective wisdom about building scalable, resilient networked systems.

sections.title: Core Principles
sections.content:
Packet Switching
The Internet is fundamentally a packet-switched network, not circuit-switched. Resources are shared statistically, enabling more efficient utilization and graceful degradation.
Fate Sharing
State should be kept at the endpoints, not in the network. If a node fails, only the connections using that node are affected, not the entire network.
Heterogeneity Support
The architecture must support a wide variety of link technologies, from carrier pigeons to fiber optics, without requiring modification.
Autonomous Design
There is no single controlling entity. The Internet is a voluntary cooperation of independently managed networks.

sections.title: The End-to-End Argument
sections.content:
Perhaps the most important principle: functions should be implemented at the endpoints of a communication, not in the intermediary network nodes. The network should be kept simple and general-purpose.

"In general, the network should provide a general transport service, and specific features should be implemented at the endpoints." This principle argues against building application-specific features into the network infrastructure.

Endpoint Function
Network Function
Error correction
Best-effort delivery
Flow control
Routing
Encryption
Forwarding
Application logic
Addressing

sections.title: Simplicity and Generality
sections.content:
The Internet architecture values simplicity and generality. Protocols should be designed to be as simple as possible while still meeting requirements.

Postel's Law
"Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send." - Jon Postel. This robustness principle has been fundamental to Internet interoperability.
Minimal Design
Keep it simple. When in doubt, leave it out. Features that are not strictly necessary add complexity and potential failure modes.
Protocol Independence
Each protocol layer should be independent. Changes at one layer should not require changes at another.

sections.title: Layering
sections.content:
The Internet protocol suite follows a layered architecture. Each layer provides services to the layer above and uses services from the layer below.

ApplicationHTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH - end-user protocolsLayer 7
TransportTCP, UDP - end-to-end communicationLayer 4
InternetIP - addressing and routing across networksLayer 3
LinkEthernet, Wi-Fi - local network deliveryLayer 2

While layering is a useful conceptual model, strict layering is sometimes violated for performance reasons (e.g., TCP checksum covers application data). The Internet architecture is more pragmatic than the OSI model.

sections.title: Universal Connectivity
sections.content:
The Internet was designed to provide universal connectivity - any host should be able to communicate with any other host. This principle has been eroded by NAT and firewalls but remains an architectural goal.

Network Address Translation (NAT), while solving the IPv4 address exhaustion problem, fundamentally violates the end-to-end principle and universal connectivity. IPv6 was designed to restore these properties by providing sufficient address space for every device.

The tension between universal connectivity and security continues to shape Internet architecture. Modern approaches like IPv6, STUN/TURN, and ICE attempt to balance reachability with protection.
